entries.title: The old French dish names
entries.say: As it reads: the old French dish names.
entries.summary: Classical French cooking names dishes for garnishes, regions and people, and each name promises what is on the plate: Clamart means peas, Argenteuil asparagus, Rossini foie gras and truffle. New Orleans added names of its own.
entries.guest: Florentine on a French menu means the dish comes with spinach, and Véronique means grapes: the old names tell you what is on the plate before the description does.

paras: Classical French cooking names dishes after places, people and the things that come with them, and every name is a promise: Clamart means peas before the description says so. For a Chef these names are the old kitchen's working vocabulary; for a server they answer a guest's commonest question: what does that mean?

Read a name in three parts. The main item comes first: sole, poulet (chicken), oeufs (eggs) or tournedos (TOOR-nuh-doh), a small round steak from the fillet. Then the link, à la, often dropped, so sole à la Dubarry becomes sole Dubarry. À la is short for à la mode de, in the fashion of, which is why the name after it is feminine: à la bourguignonne. Last comes the name, pointing to a garnish, a region or a person. Decide which, and you have read the plate.

Garnish names come from towns that grew a vegetable, or people tied to it. Florentine means spinach, after Florence, classically under a cheese sauce browned under the grill. Dubarry (doo-bah-REE) means cauliflower, for Madame du Barry, mistress of Louis XV. Clamart (klah-MAR) means peas and Argenteuil (ar-zhahn-TOY) asparagus, after two towns near Paris that grew them. Crécy (kray-SEE) means carrots, so potage Crécy is carrot soup. Parmentier means potato, for Antoine-Augustin Parmentier, the pharmacist who championed it in eighteenth-century France. Véronique means grapes, after Sole Véronique, poached sole with peeled green grapes.

Style names point to a region and its larder. Bourguignonne (boor-geen-YUN), Burgundy style, means red wine, lardons (small batons of bacon), mushrooms and small glazed onions; in boeuf bourguignon the word turns masculine to agree with boeuf. Lyonnaise means onions cooked golden in butter. Provençale means tomato, garlic and olive oil. Normande means Normandy's cream, and on many menus its apples or cider. Forestière, from the forest, means mushrooms. Grenobloise (greh-noh-BLWAHZ) means capers and lemon, usually with brown butter and croutons, on fish.

Names for people flatter a patron or a star. Rossini (roh-SEE-nee), for the composer Gioachino Rossini, means foie gras, fattened duck or goose liver, and truffle: tournedos Rossini sits on a fried crouton under a slice of each, with a Madeira sauce. Soubise (soo-BEEZ), for the Prince de Soubise, a marshal of France under Louis XV, means a purée of onions. Mornay means coated in a cheese sauce and browned, though whose name it carries is disputed. Chateaubriand (shah-toh-bree-AHN), for the writer and statesman François-René de Chateaubriand, is a thick cut from the centre of the fillet.

New Orleans kept the habit. Hussarde, hussar style, means poached eggs on Canadian bacon over a toasted base, with marchand de vin, a red wine sauce, beneath and hollandaise on top; a recipe was printed in 1895, credited to a New York hotel chef, and Brennan's made it famous from about 1950. Sardou, named at Antoine's for the playwright Victorien Sardou, began as poached eggs on artichoke bottoms with hollandaise, finished with ham, anchovy and truffle; most later versions dropped those for creamed spinach. Rockefeller, also Antoine's, means oysters baked under a rich green sauce, named for John D. Rockefeller for its richness.

Bienville, for the city's founder, means oysters under a shrimp and mushroom cream sauce, most often credited to Arnaud's, though Antoine's has claimed it too. Pontchartrain names the lake north of the city, itself named for a minister of Louis XIV; on menus it often means fish topped with crabmeat. Clemenceau, for Georges Clemenceau, who led France at the end of the First World War, means chicken with fried potatoes, mushrooms, peas and garlic, most often credited to Galatoire's.

Some names have drifted, and a Chef knows both meanings. Eggs Florentine on an American brunch menu is usually a Benedict with spinach in place of the ham. Classical sole normande came with oysters, mussels, shrimp and mushrooms under sauce normande, a fish velouté (fish stock thickened with a blond roux) enriched with egg yolks and cream, and no apples. Chateaubriand was a thick grilled steak; many menus now roast the centre cut whole for two. Most copies of Oysters Rockefeller use spinach, though Antoine's has said its own sauce holds none. The house decides what its name means, so read its description too.

At the table, say the name, then what it means in plain English: “Florentine means it comes on spinach.” Never use a name to show off, and never correct a guest who says it differently. Unsure how the house makes a named dish? Ask the kitchen rather than promise the classic.

faults.fault: Promising a guest the classical dish from the name alone
faults.cause: Names drift: an American eggs Florentine or a farmhouse normande is not the classical plate.
faults.fix: Read the house description, describe that, and ask the kitchen when the two disagree.

faults.fault: Telling a legend as a record
faults.cause: Stories grow after the dish: Oysters Bienville is credited to Arnaud's, yet Antoine's has claimed it too.
faults.fix: Say named for, not invented by, and give both claims where houses disagree.

faults.cause: Clamart, Crécy and Argenteuil are all place names, and none sounds like its vegetable.
faults.fix: Learn them as pairs: Clamart peas, Crécy carrots, Argenteuil asparagus, Dubarry cauliflower.

sources.title: A Guide to Modern Cookery, A. Escoffier (London: Heinemann, 1907)
Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne, sieur de Bienville, Encyclopaedia Britannica

cards.front: What three things can the name in a classical dish title point to?
cards.back: A garnish, such as Clamart for peas; a regional style, such as provençale; or a person, such as Rossini for foie gras and truffle.

cards.front: What does à la mean in a dish name, and why is the next word feminine?
cards.back: In the style of. It is short for à la mode de, and the name agrees with mode, so à la bourguignonne.

cards.front: Which vegetable does each promise: Clamart, Argenteuil, Crécy, Dubarry?
cards.back: Clamart peas, Argenteuil asparagus, Crécy carrots, Dubarry cauliflower: three places that grew them and a royal mistress.

cards.front: What does Florentine promise, and how has the name drifted?
cards.back: Spinach. Classically spinach under a browned Mornay; on American brunch menus eggs Florentine is usually a Benedict with spinach in place of the ham.

cards.front: What does Parmentier promise, and who was he?
cards.back: Potato, for Antoine-Augustin Parmentier, the pharmacist who championed the potato in eighteenth-century France.

cards.front: What does Véronique promise on a menu?
cards.back: Grapes, after Sole Véronique: poached sole with peeled green grapes, so any dish à la Véronique carries grapes.

cards.front: What do bourguignonne, lyonnaise and provençale put on the plate?
cards.back: Bourguignonne: red wine, lardons, mushrooms and small onions. Lyonnaise: onions cooked golden. Provençale: tomato, garlic and olive oil.

cards.front: What does à la grenobloise (greh-noh-BLWAHZ) promise on a fish?
cards.back: Capers and lemon, usually in brown butter with small croutons: sharp and nutty against a mild fish.

cards.front: What do Rossini and Soubise promise, and who were they?
cards.back: Rossini, for the composer Gioachino Rossini, means foie gras and truffle; Soubise, for a marshal of France under Louis XV, means a soft onion purée.

cards.front: What is Chicken Clemenceau, and who is it named for?
cards.back: Chicken with fried potatoes, mushrooms, peas and garlic, most often credited to Galatoire's; named for Georges Clemenceau, who led France through the last year of the First World War.

cards.front: What do Bienville and Rockefeller promise on a New Orleans menu?
cards.back: Baked oysters. Bienville, for the city's founder, under a shrimp and mushroom cream sauce, claimed by Arnaud's and Antoine's; Rockefeller, for the magnate, under a rich green sauce.

cards.front: How should a server handle a classical name whose meaning has drifted?
cards.back: Read the house description too, say what the dish is in plain English, and ask the kitchen when unsure rather than promise the classic.

questions.q: On a classical French menu, which vegetable does the name Clamart promise?
questions.why: Clamart, a town near Paris, grew peas for the city; Crécy promises carrots, Argenteuil asparagus and Dubarry cauliflower.

questions.q: Why does a French menu print à la bourguignonne with a feminine ending?
questions.answer: It agrees with mode, from à la mode de
distractors: Every French dish name is feminine
It agrees with the word for sauce
questions.why: À la is short for à la mode de, in the fashion of, so the name agrees with mode; boeuf bourguignon alone turns masculine.

questions.q: A tournedos Rossini is ordered. What does the name promise on the steak?
questions.why: Rossini, for the composer, means foie gras and truffle; spinach is Florentine, capers and lemon grenobloise, mushrooms forestière.

questions.q: On an American brunch menu, what does eggs Florentine usually mean?
questions.answer: A Benedict with spinach in place of ham
distractors: Eggs baked with tomato and garlic
Eggs scrambled with peas and onion
questions.why: The name still promises spinach, but the American dish has drifted from the classical spinach under a browned Mornay.

questions.q: Which garnish does à la grenobloise promise on a fish?
questions.answer: Capers and lemon in brown butter
questions.why: Grenobloise means capers and lemon, usually with brown butter and croutons; grapes are Véronique, red wine bourguignonne, tomato provençale.

questions.q: Chicken with fried potatoes, mushrooms, peas and garlic carries whose name?
questions.why: Chicken Clemenceau, most often credited to Galatoire's, honours Georges Clemenceau, who led France through the last year of the First World War; Sardou and Rossini name other dishes, and Parmentier promises potato alone.

questions.q: Oysters Bienville carry the name of which person?
questions.why: Bienville founded New Orleans; the magnate is Rockefeller, the playwright Sardou and the prime minister Clemenceau.

questions.q: What does the name Parmentier promise in a classical dish?
questions.why: Parmentier honours the pharmacist who championed the potato in France; the name has nothing to do with Parmesan cheese.

questions.q: A guest asks whether our Redfish Véronique is the French classic. What should the server do?
questions.answer: Describe our version and say how it differs
distractors: Promise peeled grapes in a creamy sauce
Say the French name again, more slowly
Explain that a dish name always means one plate
questions.why: Names drift and each house decides: ours has Gulf redfish, hibiscus-pickled grapes and a preserved lemon beurre blanc, so describe that.

entries.title: Say it: the Brennan's menu
entries.say: As it reads: say it, the Brennan's menu.
entries.summary: The house's say-it list: the French and Louisiana words a server says most on the Brennan's menu, each with the house guide's respelling, from hollandaise and Hussarde to roux and pralines, and the habit of saying each name, then what it is.
entries.guest: Our Eggs Hussarde, hussar style, is poached eggs on Canadian bacon with a red wine sauce beneath and hollandaise on top: New Orleans' answer to Eggs Benedict.

paras: This is the say-it list for our menu: the French and Louisiana words a new server or cook says every shift, with the house guide's respellings. A respelling writes the word the way an American dining room says it, with the stressed syllable in capitals: bair-NAYZ. A name said cleanly tells a guest you know the plate; a name stumbled over makes them doubt the rest. One habit goes with every name: say it, then say what it is in plain English.

Start with the sauces, because they name most of the plates. Hollandaise, HOL-un-dayz, is the buttery, lemony egg-yolk sauce of Eggs Benedict. Béarnaise, bair-NAYZ, is hollandaise's cousin: egg yolk and butter sharpened with a reduction of vinegar, shallot and tarragon, the classic sauce for steak. Choron, sho-ROHN, is béarnaise with tomato. Foyot, fwah-YO, is béarnaise made richer with a reduced beef glaze. Marchand de vin, mar-SHAHN duh VAN, the wine merchant's sauce, is a savoury red wine and mushroom sauce; whether tonight's carries mushroom or ham is a question for the chef. Beurre blanc, burr BLAHN, is a silky white wine and butter sauce, with no K sound at the end.

Then the dishes. Hussarde, hoo-SARD, means hussar style. Sardou, sar-DOO, carries the name of a French playwright. Véronique, vay-ro-NEEK, means with grapes. En papillote, ahn pah-pee-YOHT, means in paper, though our Gulf Fish en Papillote is wrapped in banana leaf. Poussin, poo-SAN, means young chicken: our Poussin à la Moutarde uses a Cornish hen, the nearest American bird, brined in sweet tea, fried and sauced with mustard cream. Chateaubriand, shah-toh-bree-AHN, is the thick centre cut of the beef tenderloin, roasted for two.

The Louisiana words come next. Roux, ROO, is flour cooked in fat and stirred, white or blond for French sauces and taken to a dark brown for gumbo and turtle soup; the darker it goes, the more flavour and the less thickening, and how dark ours goes is a question for the chef. Andouille, ahn-DOO-ee, is the smoky Louisiana pork sausage in our gumbo; tell a guest who avoids pork that it is in the gumbo before they order. Tasso, TAH-so, is Cajun spiced, cured and smoked pork that seasons the sauce of the shrimp and grits.

Guests in this city ask about étouffée, ay-too-FAY, so know it whether or not tonight's menu carries it: it means smothered, crawfish or shrimp cooked down in a thick sauce over rice. Pralines, PRAH-leen, are the pecan and brown sugar candies that add crunch to our bread pudding. Café brûlot, ka-FAY broo-LOH, is the city's spiced, flamed coffee, whose flavours our coffee cake borrows.

Four words trip people. Débris, DAY-bree, is meltingly tender slow-cooked meat in its own gravy: on the Eggs Owen, short rib braised in red wine. Brabant, bra-BAHNT, names our crisp cubed potatoes. Mignonette, min-yo-NET, is the raw bar sauce of vinegar, shallot and cracked pepper for oysters. Fines herbes, feen ZAIRB, with the S of fines carried onto herbes, is the classic French mix of parsley, chives, tarragon and chervil, on the crab claws.

Some words are said two ways; follow the house. The guide gives Hussarde as hoo-SARD, though hoo-ZARD is heard. It gives mignonette as min-yo-NET, and meen-yo-NET, nearer the French, is also heard. Tasso is TAH-so, though TASS-oh is heard too. Brabant is bra-BAHNT in the guide, bra-BAHN in French and bruh-BANT to many locals. Pralines are PRAH-leen, never PRAY-leen. Which the floor uses for Hussarde, tasso and Brabant is a question for the manager at lineup, the short meeting before service. Until then, use the guide's respelling, and never correct a guest.

Three names carry a story the house wants told with care. Eggs Hussarde is our signature, but the dish is older than the restaurant, so never say it was invented here. Eggs Sardou was created at Antoine's; ours is Antoine's dish in the Brennan's style, with crispy artichokes, Parmesan creamed spinach and Choron. Redfish Véronique keeps the grapes of the French classic and pickles them in hibiscus.

At the table, say the name once, clearly, then the plain English: “The Sardou, sar-DOO, is poached eggs over crispy artichokes and Parmesan creamed spinach, with a tomato béarnaise.” Never use the French to show off, and never make a guest feel wrong for saying it differently. If a guest asks what goes into a sauce, give the description, and send any allergy question to the kitchen.

faults.fault: Saying burr BLANK for beurre blanc
faults.cause: Reading the French spelling as if it were English.
faults.fix: Say burr BLAHN: the final C is silent, as the house notes.

faults.cause: The pronunciation common outside New Orleans.
faults.fix: Say PRAH-leen, the house habit, never PRAY-leen.

faults.cause: Treating the house respelling as the only right way to say a word.
faults.fix: Say it the house way yourself and let the guest's version stand.

brennans.how: Say hoo-SARD, then: poached eggs on Canadian bacon with marchand de vin beneath and hollandaise on top, New Orleans' answer to Eggs Benedict. Call it our signature, never invented here.

Say sar-DOO, then: poached eggs with crispy artichokes, Parmesan creamed spinach and Choron. Created at Antoine's and named for the playwright Victorien Sardou; ours is Antoine's dish in the Brennan's style.
Say vay-ro-NEEK, then: with grapes. Our Redfish Véronique carries hibiscus-pickled grapes and a preserved lemon beurre blanc in place of the classic's fresh grapes and creamy sauce.
Say fwah-YO, then: béarnaise made even richer with a reduced beef glaze. On the Roasted Chateaubriand it brings the depth that the lean tenderloin lacks.
The guide prints bra-BAHNT; the French say bra-BAHN and many locals bruh-BANT, so confirm the floor's habit at lineup. Then: crisp fried potato cubes, a New Orleans classic.
Say min-yo-NET, then: shallot and cracked pepper in vinegar. Ours carries preserved Fresno chilli and parsley on the Grand Isle Jewel oysters, spooned on by the guest at the table.

sources.title: A Guide to Modern Cookery, A. Escoffier (London: Heinemann, 1907)

cards.front: Say Poussin à la Moutarde the house way, then say what it is.
cards.back: poo-SAN, young chicken, then the plain English: ours is a sweet tea-brined Cornish hen, fried and sauced with mustard cream, with turnips and shallots.

cards.front: How do you say hollandaise, béarnaise and beurre blanc?
cards.back: HOL-un-dayz, bair-NAYZ and burr BLAHN, with no K sound at the end of blanc.

cards.front: How do you say Choron and Foyot, and what is each?
cards.back: Choron, sho-ROHN, is béarnaise with tomato, on the Sardou. Foyot, fwah-YO, is béarnaise with a reduced beef glaze, on the Chateaubriand.

cards.front: How do you say marchand de vin, and what is it?
cards.back: mar-SHAHN duh VAN, the wine merchant's sauce: a savoury red wine brown sauce under the egg on the Eggs Hussarde; confirm mushroom or ham with the chef.

cards.front: How do you say Hussarde, and what must you never say about it?
cards.back: hoo-SARD. It is our signature, but the dish is older than the restaurant, so never say it was invented here.

cards.front: How do you say Sardou, and where was the dish created?
cards.back: sar-DOO. It was created at Antoine's and named for the playwright Victorien Sardou; ours is Antoine's dish in the Brennan's style.

cards.front: How do you say Véronique, and what does it mean on our menu?
cards.back: vay-ro-NEEK: with grapes. Our Redfish Véronique carries hibiscus-pickled grapes and a preserved lemon beurre blanc.

cards.front: How do you say roux, andouille and tasso?
cards.back: ROO, ahn-DOO-ee and TAH-so: flour cooked in fat, the smoky pork sausage in the gumbo, and the spiced, smoked pork that seasons the shrimp and grits.

cards.front: How does the house say pralines?
cards.back: PRAH-leen, never PRAY-leen: the pecan and brown sugar candies that add crunch to our bread pudding.

cards.front: How do you say débris and fines herbes?
cards.back: DAY-bree, slow-cooked meat in its own gravy, as on the Eggs Owen; and feen ZAIRB, parsley, chives, tarragon and chervil, with the S of fines carried over.

cards.front: What do you do when a word is said two ways, like Hussarde, tasso or Brabant?
cards.back: Use the house guide's respelling, hoo-SARD, TAH-so and bra-BAHNT, ask the manager at lineup which the floor uses, and never correct a guest.

cards.front: How does the house guide respell mignonette, and what else is heard?
cards.back: min-yo-NET, with meen-yo-NET, nearer the French, also heard. It is vinegar, shallot and cracked pepper for oysters.

questions.q: How should a server say beurre blanc at the table?
questions.why: The final C of blanc is silent and the stress falls on the second word, so it is burr BLAHN, with no K sound.

questions.q: A guest asks whether Brennan's invented Eggs Hussarde. What is the right answer?
questions.answer: It is our signature, but the dish is older than us
distractors: Yes, it was first created here in this kitchen
No, it was created at Antoine's, like the Sardou
Nobody knows where or when it was first made
questions.why: A recipe for eggs à la Hussarde was printed before Brennan's opened; the house made it famous, so call it our signature, never our invention.

questions.q: How does the house say pralines?
questions.why: The house guide gives PRAH-leen, never PRAY-leen, the pronunciation common outside New Orleans.

questions.q: Which sauce is béarnaise made richer with a reduced beef glaze, served on the Chateaubriand?
questions.why: Foyot, fwah-YO, adds meat glaze to béarnaise; Choron adds tomato, marchand de vin is a red wine sauce and beurre blanc a butter sauce.

questions.q: How is Véronique, as in our Redfish Véronique, said in the dining room?
questions.why: The house guide gives vay-ro-NEEK, the stress on the last syllable, followed by the plain English: with grapes, here hibiscus-pickled ones.

questions.q: Where was Eggs Sardou first created?
questions.why: Antoine's created the dish and named it for Victorien Sardou; ours is Antoine's dish in the Brennan's style, never a Brennan's invention.

questions.q: Tasso is heard as TAH-so and as TASS-oh. What should a new server do?
questions.answer: Use the house respelling and confirm at lineup
distractors: Correct any guest who says it the other way round
Pick whichever of the two sounds more French
Avoid saying the word at all during service
questions.why: The house guide gives TAH-so and asks the manager which the floor uses; a guest who says it the other way is never corrected.

questions.q: How is andouille said in our dining room?
questions.why: The house says ahn-DOO-ee, stress on the middle syllable and no L sound, for the smoky pork sausage in the gumbo.

questions.q: On our menu, what bird is the Poussin à la Moutarde?
questions.why: Poussin means young chicken; ours is a sweet tea-brined Cornish hen, fried, with mustard cream. The Rohan duck breast is on the dinner tasting.
